title: Sachem Tackapousha
summary: Tackapousha was a Massapequa sachem whose diplomacy linked western Long Island communities under Dutch and English rule. His career includes treaty-making, Hempstead boundary negotiations, and repeated challenges to settlers’ claims and unpaid land.
content:
A western Long Island diplomat

Tackapousha, also written Tackapausha and Tackpousha, was a seventeenth-century Massapequa sachem whose diplomacy connected western Long Island communities. Treaty and council records trace his public work from the 1650s into the 1680s. They reveal a leader maintaining alliances while repeatedly challenging claims to Native land.2 3

His story connects Merrick and Hempstead Plains with Massapequa, neighboring communities, and the colonial government at Manhattan. His birth and death dates are not established by these records.2 3

1656: an alliance with New Netherland

The agreement of March 12, 1656 joined Tackapousha with the government of New Netherland under Peter Stuyvesant. It promised a fortified trading place and linked peace with the movement of goods and people. The record names an alliance extending through Massapequa, Matinecock, Secatogue, Mericock, Rockaway, and Canarsie. It tied Dutch protection to the territorial division agreed at Hartford.1

The parties promised to include one another in peace negotiations and to deny lodging to enemies. They also agreed that wrongs against Native people by Dutch or English residents, and wrongs against settlers by Native people, should receive satisfaction through their respective leaders. The proposed trading fort was part of this larger set of reciprocal obligations.1

September 1656: keeping a fragile peace

Dutch council minutes show the everyday work behind that alliance. On September 26, officials from Brooklyn and neighboring settlements voiced fears of a Native attack while Stuyvesant was away. Four days later, Massapequa representatives brought back clothing that they said had been stolen by other Native people.2

They explained that their sachem, recorded as Tachpausan, had ordered the return. Through interpreter Lawrens Hansen, the council thanked them and promised reciprocal action when thefts were reported. The incident shows diplomacy operating through messengers, restitution, and the prevention of a larger conflict.2

1657–1659: Hempstead and South Shore boundaries

The July 4, 1657 Hempstead confirmation brought Tackapousha together with Wyandanch, Cockenoe, and other participants. The records connect an earlier purchase claim with renewed acknowledgment and the marking of boundaries. Later confirmation did not prevent further disputes over payment.3 4 5

In the Huntington records, Tackapousha appears with Wyandanch on the May 23, 1659 receipt for South Shore meadows. The earlier agreement had assigned Cockenoe the work of marking those lands. Tackapousha’s role thus extended beyond a single town or transaction.3 4 5

Quashawam’s testimony recorded in 1666 also describes kinship linking Tackapousha with her parents and sachems interested in the Cattawamnuck lands. Family connections formed part of the political landscape across which these agreements were made.3 4 5

August 5, 1675: “Mericock” had not been paid for

Before Governor Andros and the council, Tackapousha said that Hempstead had never paid for the Mericock land it occupied. The record distinguishes northern and southern claims. It also records an allegation that payment had been offered but rejected as insufficient.2

Hempstead’s representatives appealed to a Dutch patent, compensation for livestock losses, conquest, and confirmation by the Montaukett sachem. The Native parties denied that the Montaukett sachem had the right to give away their land and maintained their demand for payment. When asked what satisfaction they wanted, they requested time to consult their friends.2

This hearing preserves both the settlers’ arguments and the Native response. It demonstrates why an earlier deed or patent did not necessarily settle ownership or extinguish local objections.2

1683: another petition, still asserting possession

On October 9, 1683, the council considered Tackapousha’s petition concerning Hempstead and a disputed neck of land. It ordered Hempstead’s inhabitants to appear and explain why Native possessions were being disturbed and building obstructed. When they appeared on October 22, the matter was referred to the Court of Assizes.2

Across changes from Dutch to English rule, Tackapousha continued to use councils and negotiations to assert Native interests. His recorded career is a history of sustained political work, including demands that colonial purchasers answer for their promises.2

why_this_matters: Tackapousha places Merrick and western Long Island history within Native leadership, diplomacy, and contested land records. His deed and court appearances show that Native people were not passive figures in colonial deeds; they negotiated, challenged, and defended land relationships under pressure.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
